A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Unified Spherical Frontend (USF) work. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, detection, segmentation, rotation-robustness and cross-lens experiments in Tables 2–7, with supplementary qualitative results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds computational benchmarks for sampling, interpolation, spherical operators and complete networks in Appendix F.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.2 revises the stated continuous-kernel embedding: v1 uses normalized distance and direction with sine/cosine features; v2 specifies cosine-only radial features with support-adapted integer frequencies and strictly periodic angular features excluding the raw angle. The overall pipeline, PWC kernels, architectures and losses remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use Spherical MNIST, PANDORA and Stanford 2D-3D-S for the same tasks, rotation scenarios and pinhole/fisheye/panoramic coverage. The added computational benchmarks do not introduce new perceptual datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds reported S2CNN and SO(3) CNN comparisons to the existing MNIST comparison. Appendix F additionally compares spherical operators against planar Conv2d and MaxPool2d. Detection and segmentation comparator membership is unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces substantial computational evaluation protocols: cold-start versus cached execution, MLP training versus inference, runtime and FLOPs, and matched network configurations. Operator comparisons use 5×5 planar kernels against approximately 25–30 spherical neighbors. Existing task splits, training budgets and accuracy metrics are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds systematic analyses of caching benefits, sampler/interpolator costs, continuous versus discrete kernels, dense versus sparse aggregation, and network overhead. v1 discussed these optimizations without measurements. The earlier rotation tests and sampler/kernel-bin ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Appendix F newly states that computational benchmark results are averaged over 10 runs. No corresponding timing experiments appeared in v1. Error bars, confidence intervals and additional seed information are not supplied, and accuracy-result uncertainty reporting remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Existing accuracy entries in Tables 2–7 are unchanged. New MNIST rows report S2CNN at 96%/94% and SO(3) CNN at 98.7%/98.1% for NR/RR. Figures 9–11 add extensive timing/FLOP results, including sustained YOLOv11 times of 641.7 ms spherical versus 21.5 ms planar. These are added results, not improvements to retained scores.

T1.justification: Section 3.2.2 adds explicit integer-frequency embedding restrictions and an argument that the radial MLP output is even and 2π-periodic; v1 did not establish these radial properties. The appendix's spherical-correlation and rotation-equivariance derivations are otherwise unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: a modular, lens-agnostic spatial spherical frontend, distance-kernel rotation equivariance, efficient processing and cross-lens generalization. Revised wording and additional evidence do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for lower FLOPs but slower execution, attributes overhead to missing optimized CUDA kernels, and justifies restricting spectral comparisons to MNIST. Appendices I–J add interpretations of retained detection orientations and full-dataset lens results. The new comparable-runtime and reduced-degradation language exceeds what Figure 11 and Table 7 consistently support.

D1.justification: v2 supplies hardware/software details for the new benchmarks: NVIDIA H200, PyTorch 2.8.0, CUDA 12.8, torch_scatter 2.1.2 and float32. It further documents implementation variants and adds a project-website pointer. Existing optimizer, augmentation, architecture and loss specifications are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds DeepSphere and Geodesic Convolutional Neural Networks to its discussion of geometry-aware approaches, plus a Bridges-2 resource citation. The new MNIST comparator papers were already cited in v1. Other reference changes mainly update bibliographic metadata without changing the underlying works.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract and selected method passages, expands computation optimization into three subsections, changes appendix numbering to A–J, moves supplementary pointers into footnotes, and adds acknowledgments and affiliation details. The overall narrative and section order remain stable.

P2.justification: v2 adds three computational benchmark charts and two rows to Table 2. The existing DeepLab architecture diagram moves from Figure 9 to Figure 12, and supplementary tables shift position. Existing diagrams and qualitative examples are retained, with limited formatting and layout adjustments.

improvement.justification: The added spherical-CNN comparisons and computational benchmarks improve empirical context and transparency beyond v1's largely qualitative efficiency discussion. Hardware, software and repeat-count details make the new evidence more assessable. The gain is limited by overinterpretation: Figure 11 shows roughly 20–30× sustained-runtime gaps despite comparable-runtime wording, while Appendix J's broad cross-lens interpretation is not consistently supported by unchanged Table 7.
